name: Follicular unit transplantation (FUT)

card.summary: Strip-harvest hair transplant: a scalp strip is removed and dissected into grafts, leaving a thin linear donor scar.
card.aka: FUT, strip harvesting, strip surgery, FUSS
card.note: Leaves a linear donor scar, which is the main reason many patients choose FUE instead.

quick.overview:
Follicular unit transplantation removes a thin strip of hair-bearing skin from the back of the scalp, which technicians dissect under microscopes into natural follicular units for implanting in balding areas.

It became the standard hair transplant approach in the 1990s and is often compared with follicular unit extraction (FUE), which avoids a strip incision.
quick.mechanism: Grafts from the donor zone retain resistance to pattern hair loss, so transplanted hairs are described as lasting. The strip method allows many grafts from a single session, with the wound closed by sutures.
quick.risks: The donor site retains a thin linear scar that is usually concealed by surrounding hair. Recovery includes stitches or staples and about two weeks of healing; shock loss and other graft-related effects are described.

lead: Follicular unit transplantation (FUT), also called strip harvesting, strip surgery or FUSS, is a hair transplant technique used to restore hair density on a thinning or receding scalp. A strip of hair-bearing scalp is taken from the donor region at the back and sides of the head and divided under stereo-microscopes into naturally occurring follicular units of one to four hairs, which are then implanted into balding areas.[1][2][3][9]

For appearance, FUT is used to rebuild a hairline, fill thinning crowns, and restore eyebrow, beard or scar-area hair, giving a fuller and younger frame to the face. A 2020 review describes hair transplant as a reliable procedure that can give natural, high-impact results with minimal downtime.[4] Because grafts come from donor hair that resists pattern hair loss, transplanted hair is generally described as lasting.[1]

The method leaves a thin linear donor scar that is typically hidden by surrounding hair; scarring from strip excision was the motivation for the 2002 paper that introduced follicular unit extraction (FUE), the main alternative.[2] Within hair-restoration practice, surgeons and patient groups describe FUT as better suited to some patients than FUE, for example people who keep their hair long or have very advanced hair loss.[9]

paras: The scalp is numbed, usually with sedation, and a strip is removed from the donor area and the wound closed with sutures or staples. A team dissects the strip into grafts, recipient sites are created in the thinning area, and the grafts are placed in them.[9] Wikipedia gives a typical strip size of about 1 to 1.5 cm by 15 to 30 cm, with sutures removed after about two weeks unless dissolvable stitches are used.[1] Before surgery, surgeons assess scalp laxity and existing hair density, and patients may be advised to stop medications that increase bleeding; some are advised to use topical minoxidil beforehand.[1]

A 2021 overview in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology describes modern hair restoration as based on follicular unit transplantation, in which follicular units are the exclusive grafts, and discusses how to identify good and poor candidates, since not all hair disorders are suitable for transplantation.[3] The 2020 review in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics focuses on performing the technique specifically.[4]

Early skin and hair grafting is attributed to Menahem Hodara, who transplanted hair onto favus scars in 1897, and to Japanese surgeons in the 1930s such as Okuda, who grafted eyebrows and lashes.[1] The New York dermatologist Norman Orentreich showed that transplanted hair keeps the characteristics of its donor site, a principle he called donor dominance; the technique he used was nicknamed the cookie cutter method, and by 1966 about 10,000 men worldwide had been treated.[10]

Plug grafting gave way to strip excision with microscopic dissection in the 1980s, with Carlos Uebel and William Rassman popularising micrografts and B. L. Limmer using stereo-microscopes to split strips.[1] Walter Unger described the safe donor zone in 1994.[1] A 2020 review notes that earlier techniques such as hair plugs and scalp reductions left a negative public impression of hair restoration, which follicular-unit techniques sought to move beyond.[4]

FUT leaves a linear scar in the donor area. Surgeons may use a trichophytic closure, in which hair from the wound edge grows through the scar to make it harder to see; Wikipedia says this is thought to give a finer scar.[1][9] The International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery says scars can be corrected afterwards by re-excision, by transplanting into the scar, or by scalp micropigmentation, and that scars tend to heal better with age.[9] Because the donor area is not shaved, it stays covered during recovery, and discomfort is often described as lower than with FUE, although some patients have more pain.[9] Temporary shedding of native hair, called shock loss, can occur after transplant surgery and usually resolves.[1][9]

In FUE individual units are removed with small punches of roughly 0.6 to 1.2 mm, leaving small scattered scars instead of one linear scar. Wikipedia says FUE involves longer surgery, higher cost and, according to some surgeons, a lower proportion of successful grafts; recovery is shorter, under a week.[1][9] The ISHRS notes that FUT is generally faster and usually cheaper because it takes less surgeon labour, does not require shaving, and carries no risk of overharvesting the donor area.[9] Robotic systems have been developed to assist FUE harvesting.[1][5]

Patient groups described as suited to FUT include people who wear their hair long and do not want to shave, older patients whose scars heal better, and people with advanced hair loss (Norwood 6 or 7), where a strip can yield more grafts from the centre of a narrow donor zone.[9]

Price depends on the number of grafts. Wikipedia cites an average of about US$1.07 per graft in Turkey and US$7.00 in Canada, and a UK range of GBP 1,000 to 30,000.[1] A 2021 German review notes that no defined specialist standard exists for hair transplantation and recommends thorough informed consent and consultation to avoid patient dissatisfaction.[6] Hair transplant is often paired with medical hair-loss treatment; a 2021 review discusses combination approaches.[11]

A randomised double-blind study in 10 patients compared three strip dissection techniques (Haber's, Pathomvanich's and Ahmad's, using a tissue spreader, skin hooks and sharp scissors) by dividing each strip into three parts.[8] Reviews summarise FUT outcomes and complications more broadly, describing hair transplantation as a procedure with low complication risk and high benefit to patients.[3][4][6] A 2024 systematic review of 141 studies on androgenetic alopecia treatments included hair transplantation among procedures that promote hair growth and highlighted individualised, multifaceted approaches.[7] The 2002 paper introducing FUE discusses FUT donor scarring as its motivation.[2]

timeline.event: Menahem Hodara transplants hair onto favus scars.[1]
Okuda in Japan develops early hair grafting for eyebrows and lashes.[1]
Strip excision with microscopic dissection develops, replacing plug grafts.[1]
Walter Unger defines the safe donor zone.[1]
FUE introduced as an alternative to strip harvesting.[2]
Robotic FUE harvesting reviewed in Dermatologic Clinics.[5]

Dissected into follicular units and implanted in thinning areas
Transplanted hair keeps growing, restoring hairline and density
angle.text: FUT moves permanent donor hair into balding or thinning areas, which restores the hairline and overall density. It can harvest a large number of grafts in a single session, at the cost of a linear scar at the back of the head that is usually covered by hair.
